title: openTPU ships — an AI-designed FPGA inference accelerator that runs its own stack
subtitle: An independent developer published a full-stack open-source accelerator — RTL, ISA, compiler, simulator — targeting a Xilinx Kintex-7 FPGA and claims the agents designed most of it.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: A GitHub user working under the handle FeSens shipped openTPU today, a full-stack open-source inference accelerator spanning hand-written SystemVerilog RTL, a custom instruction set, a bit-exact Python simulator, a kernel compiler, a profiler named Lens, and host utilities including a chat client. The design targets a Xilinx Kintex-7 xc7k480t FPGA on an Inspur YPCB-00338 PCIe card with 4 GiB of DDR3-1066 memory across two channels. Supported models include LFM2.5-230M, several Qwen3 and Qwen3.5 variants up to 4B, SmolLM3-3B, Phi-4-mini, and Gemma 4. The author reports 59.0 tokens per second decode and 295.6 tokens per second prefill on LFM2.5-230M in int8, with DRAM running at 82–94% of a 17.1 GB/s peak.

The novelty is not the Kintex-7 numbers — any seasoned FPGA engineer can wire up a small transformer accelerator on this class of part. The novelty is the claim stamped on the README: FeSens labels openTPU as "developed by AI," meaning the RTL, the ISA, the compiler passes, and most of the host software were produced by language-model agents under human direction rather than written by hand. The project is framed as a test of whether frontier coding agents can design the chip that runs their own inference, end to end, in a single repo. Each layer is open and inspectable: readers can judge for themselves which parts look agent-generated and which look human-authored.

This matters because the self-hosting story has been a stated milestone for frontier labs for a year. OpenAI's internal rumors around AI-assisted silicon, Anthropic's writeups on agents operating lab infrastructure, and Google's claims about Gemini contributing to TPU design all point in the same direction. openTPU is the first public artifact that lets outsiders audit the whole stack rather than take a press release's word for it. The scale is small — a Kintex-7 is a hobbyist-grade part, not a wafer-scale accelerator — but the fact that a solo developer with agent assistance can produce a working, documented accelerator is itself a signal about where the floor of hardware design has moved in 2026.

A takeaway for learners: open projects like this are the fastest way to actually understand how an AI accelerator works, because the whole stack is readable in one afternoon. Clone the repo, read the ISA document, trace one matmul from the compiler through the simulator into the RTL, and you will know more about transformer hardware than most people who read the datasheet of a commercial part. Then ask: which commits look like they were written by an agent? That exercise is better interview prep than any benchmark leaderboard.
